Reduced acidification elevates measured Golgi pH in cultured mouse embryonic fibroblasts.
Golgi homeostasis affects enzyme activity, localization and transit time; different glycan modifications may increase or decrease.
Altered acidity is implicated in membrane transport, but a pH-independent contribution has not been excluded.
The mouse brain glycosylation defect is associated with V0a2 dysfunction; its tissue-specific relationship to pH remains unresolved.
Altered N-glycan terminal processing changes transferrin isoforms; the profile can be normal in early infancy.
The authors proposed defective VWF glycosylation and multimerization, while also considering abnormal matrix interaction. This is a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated causal link.
Secretory-pathway dysfunction is associated with tropoelastin retention; premature coacervation and impaired carrier recruitment are proposed intermediates.
Reduced secretion and abnormal extracellular aggregates limit mature elastin accumulation.
Tropoelastin storage accompanies cell death; causation from the aggregate itself was proposed rather than isolated experimentally.
Impaired matrix deposition contributes to rarefied and abnormal dermal elastic fibers.
Loss of elastogenic cells is a proposed additional contributor; its quantitative tissue contribution is unmeasured.
Abnormal dermal elastic fibers impair skin recoil.
Defective dystroglycan glycosylation plausibly weakens laminin interactions; the study associates these findings without a targeted rescue experiment.
Loss of the pial boundary permits focal neuronal overmigration in the proposed developmental mechanism.
Abnormal cortical organization is the predicted tissue consequence of disturbed migration.

Both mouse models exhibit focal neuronal overmigration into cortical layer I, especially in frontal cortex. The R755Q model is more severely affected despite its smaller measured MEF pH shift. Developmental dysgenesis may contribute to neurologic manifestations, but does not fully explain later regression.
